**AND**

Any **one** of the following:

- Electrons pass down the electron transport chain **AND** release energy; **[1 mark]**
- Hydrogen ions are pumped / actively transported across the inner mitochondrial membrane / into the intermembrane space; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *While the details of the events during oxidative phosphorylation can be quite difficult to get your head around, Fig. 1 provides helpful scaffolding here to allow you to describe process W one step at a time. Just make sure that you follow the instructions in the question and identify X, Y and Z to gain full marks here.*

> *You might be tempted to refer to the process of chemiosmosis at this point, however, chemiosmosis is the movement of ions across a selectively permeable membrane (process W), coupled with the synthesis of ATP (not part of process W).*

Oxidative phosphorylation is affected by temperature because;

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- ATP synthase/P is an enzyme **AND **enzyme activity is affected by temperature; **[1 mark]**
- Temperature affects kinetic energy (of substrate molecules) **OR** molecules have more kinetic energy at high temperatures / less kinetic energy at low temperatures; **[1 mark]**
- Enzymes denature at high temperatures; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- Diffusion occurs faster as temperatures increase; **[1 mark]**
- Molecules move around more / faster when more kinetic energy is available; **[1 mark]**
- Hydrogen ions diffuse more quickly back across the membrane / via ATP synthase **SO** more ATP is synthesised per unit time / in a shorter time; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- Membrane permeability increases at high temperatures; **[1 mark]**
- At high temperatures the hydrogen ion gradient may become less steep / (more) hydrogen ions will be able to leak across the membrane (without passing through ATP synthase); **[1 mark]**
- At (very) high temperatures the membrane may break apart **SO** no hydrogen ions can be pumped across the membrane / no hydrogen ion gradient will be generated / chemiosmosis will stop; **[1 mark]**

*Allow H*<sup>*+*</sup>* for hydrogen ion.*

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Note that this is an 'explain' question, so you need to **explain** one aspect of the effect of temperature on oxidative phosphorylation, rather than just listing the reasons why temperature may affect rate.*

> *Any chemical reaction that relies on enzymes will be affected by changes in temperature; at **low temperatures substrate molecules have low kinetic energy**, so fewer collisions occur and **fewer enzyme-substrate complexes** **form**, resulting in a reduced rate of reaction. As kinetic energy levels increase the rate of reaction will therefore also increase. This increase in reaction rate occurs until temperatures become too high, at which point the **enzymes may denature** and the reaction will slow down and eventually stop.*

> *Diffusion is affected by temperature as **molecules with more kinetic energy move around faster**; this means that more hydrogen ions will move through ATP synthase per unit time, producing ATP at a faster rate.*

> *Reactions that occur across membranes are also affected by temperature, as temperature can affect the fluidity, and therefore the 'leakiness' of a membrane (phospholipids with more kinetic energy will move around more and be less tightly packed together). A leaky inner mitochondrial membrane will allow **hydrogen ions to leak back across the membrane**, reducing the steepness of the gradient and **reducing the rate at which ions diffuse via ATP synthase**. At very high temperatures the **membrane may break apart** altogether and there will be no chemiosmosis at all.*

In addition to the processes outlined in part b) the light dependent reactions of photosynthesis also involve the processes of oxidation and reduction.

Explain where oxidation and reduction occur during the light dependent reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
Oxidation and reduction occur in the light-dependent reactions in the following ways...

*Oxidation:*

**Final answer:** **A maximum of ****two**** of the following:**

- Chlorophyll *a*/the primary pigment/the reaction centre is oxidised when electrons are lost (during photoactivation) and passed to the electron transport chain/an electron carrier; **[1 mark]**
- Electron carriers/proteins of the electron transport/transfer chain molecules are oxidised when they pass on/give up electrons to the next electron carrier/photosystem/NADP; **[1 mark]**
- Water is oxidised when it loses electrons during photolysis; **[1 mark]**

*Reduction:*

**Final answer:** **A maximum of**** two**** of the following:**

- Electron carriers/proteins of the electron transport/transfer chain are reduced when they accept/gain electrons from the photosystem / another electron carrier; **[1 mark]**
- Chlorophyll a is reduced when it gains/accepts electrons from an electron carrier during cyclic photophosphorylation / from water during non-cyclic photophosphorylation; **[1 mark]**
- NADP is reduced when it accepts/gains electrons (along with hydrogen ions), becoming reduced NADP or NADPH; **[1 mark]**

***Reject**** references to NAD or NADH throughout*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Oxidation is the loss (OIL) of electrons while reduction is the gain (RIG) of electrons. When chlorophyll **a**, an electron carrier protein, or water loses electrons and passes them elsewhere they are said to be **oxidised **and have taken part in an oxidation reaction. When an electron carrier, chlorophyll a, or NADP gain an electron from elsewhere they are said to be **reduced **and have taken part in a reduction reaction. It is also worth noting that it is not only electrons that are involved in oxidation and reduction reactions, they also apply to the loss or gain of hydrogen and oxygen. *

> *Note that the question asks you to **explain** the oxidation and reduction processes, so a bit more detail is required for each mark than just stating where electrons have been lost or gained. *

- Cyclic **AND** non-cyclic (photophosphorylation); **[1 mark]**

(ii) A comparison between the two types of photophosphorylation would include...

*Similarities*

- <u>Both</u> involves photosystem I; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Both</u> result in the production of ATP / involve chemiosmosis / diffusion of protons via ATP synthase; **[1 mark]**
- Photoactivation occurs in <u>both</u> cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation; **[1 mark]**

*Differences*

**Final answer:** **A maximum of ****three ****of the following:**

- In cyclic photophosphorylation only photosystem/PS I is involved **WHILE** in non-cyclic photophosphorylation both photosystem/PS I and photosystem/PS II are involved; **[1 mark]**
- In cyclic photophosphorylation only ATP is synthesised **WHILE** in non-cyclic photophosphorylation ATP and reduced NADP/NADPH are synthesised; **[1 mark]**
- In cyclic photophosphorylation the excited electrons return to the original photosystem **WHILE** in non-cyclic photophosphorylation they pass to another photosystem; **[1 mark]**
- Non-cyclic photophosphorylation involves the photolysis of water **WHILE** cyclic photophosphorylation does not; **[1 mark]**

> *The command word 'compare' requires a summary of similarities and/or differences, so you should aim to give a balance of both types of point where possible.*

> *Remember that similarities must clearly refer to both sides of the comparison, while differences must clearly present contrasting features; this can be achieved by using language such as 'both' and 'while' as shown above.*

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
The changes in carbon dioxide occur because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****five**** of the following:**

- There is a high(er) concentration of carbon dioxide at night (at all heights) **AS** photosynthesis stops at night / in the dark;** [1 mark]**
- Photosynthesis stops in the dark **AS **light energy is required for photolysis / splitting water molecules; **[1 mark]**
- There is a high(er) concentration of carbon dioxide at night **AS** organisms (continue to) produce carbon dioxide during respiration / respiration rate is higher than the rate of photosynthesis (when it is dark); **[1 mark]**
- During the day carbon dioxide levels are low(er) **AS** plants use carbon dioxide during photosynthesis; **[1 mark]**
- During the day carbon dioxide levels are low(er) **AS **rate of photosynthesis is greater than rate of respiration; **[1 mark]**
- There is a decrease in carbon dioxide concentration with height **AS** at ground level there are fewer leaves / is less light / rate of photosynthesis is lower; **[1 mark]**
- Carbon dioxide is denser than other gases in air **SO** sinks towards the ground; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Note that this is an 'explain' question so each statement must have an element of explanation to achieve a mark.*

> *Photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide while respiration produces it. During the night photosynthesis stops, so the rate of uptake of carbon dioxide decreases. During the day photosynthesis occurs at a greater rate than respiration, using carbon dioxide and causing levels to fall. The fall will be greatest in the regions of the woodland where the most photosynthesis is occurring; this is likely to be high in the canopy where light levels are high and there are many leaves.*

A group of students wanted to investigate the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis. They followed the procedure below:

1. Prepare a chloroplast suspension using an isolation medium.
2. Set up a series of test tubes in a water bath at 20 °C.
3. Set up the following tubes for the purposes of control or reference:

  - Tube **X** = 5 cm<sup>3</sup> DCPIP + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> water + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> liquid isolation medium
  - Tube **Y** = 5 cm<sup>3</sup> DCPIP + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> water + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> chloroplast suspension, wrapped in aluminium foil
  - Tube **Z** = 5.5 cm<sup>3</sup> water + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> chloroplast suspension
4. Set up another series of tubes containing 5 cm<sup>3</sup> DCPIP + 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> water.
5. Take one of the second series of tubes and place it 5 cm away from a lamp. Add 0.5 cm<sup>3</sup> chloroplast suspension and start a timer.
6. Time how long it takes for the DCPIP to become colourless.
7. Repeat steps 6-7 at different distances from the lamp, e.g. 10 cm, 15 cm, 20 cm, 25 cm, 30 cm

It is important that the isolation medium used in step 1 is at the same solute concentration as the spinach cells.

Explain why this is the case.
parts.solutionMd:

- This prevents water from moving into / out of the <u>chloroplasts</u> by osmosis; **[1 mark]**
- Prevents damage to the chloroplast membranes / prevents the chloroplasts from bursting; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember here that it is the activity of the chloroplasts that is being investigated so it doesn't matter if the plant cells themselves are damaged: in fact, it is likely that they may already have been damaged during the preparation of the chloroplast suspension. It is the chloroplast function that needs to be maintained: if they burst then all of the components that need to be close together for photosynthesis to occur will be dispersed and the reaction will not happen as normal.*

**Fig. 3**

(i) Identify the precise stage of photosynthesis in algae chloroplasts that is affected by an increased salt concentration.

[1]

(ii) Using information in Fig. 3, explain the effect that increasing salt concentration has on oxygen production in algae chloroplasts.

[2]

(iii) Explain how the effect shown in Fig. 3 will affect other aspects of the photosynthesis reactions.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The precise stage of photosynthesis in algae chloroplasts that is affected by an increased salt concentration is...

- <u>Non-cyclic</u> photophosphorylation; **[1 mark]**

> *PSII is only involved with non-cyclic photophosphorylation, so a reduction in oxygen production by PSII indicates that this stage of photosynthesis has been disrupted.*

(ii) The effect that increasing salt concentration has on photosynthesis in algae chloroplast can be explained as follows:

- Salt concentration affects the activity of the enzyme / active site / oxygen-evolving complex on photosystem/PS II; **[1 mark]**
- Salt concentration affects the rate of photolysis; **[1 mark]**

> *PSII contains an **enzyme** that catalyses the breakdown of water through photolysis; a reduction in the activity of this enzyme will **slow down photolysis** and result in reduced oxygen production.*

(iii) The effect shown in Fig. 3 will affect other parts of the photosynthesis reactions as follows:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- Fewer electrons will be released **SO** the electrons lost from PSII will not be replaced and non-cyclic photophosphorylation will stop / be slowed further; **[1 mark]**
- Fewer hydrogen ions will be released **SO **less NADP will be reduced / less NADPH will be produced; **[1 mark]**
- Fewer hydrogen<sup> </sup>ions / reduced passage of electrons along the transport chain to generate a proton gradient **SO** less ATP generated by ATP synthase / chemiosmosis; **[1 mark]**
- Less ATP/NADPH enters the Calvin cycle **SO** less GP converted to TP / less TP recycled to RuBP; **[1 mark]**

> *A reduction in the rate of photolysis doesn't only affect oxygen production, it also means that **fewer electrons** and **fewer protons** are released. The electrons released during photolysis replace those lost from PSII during photoactivation, so a failure to replace these electrons could further slow down non-cyclic phosphorylation. The protons are used to reduce NADP and to drive the production of ATP through chemiosmosis via ATP synthase. A** reduction in ATP and NADPH** production will have a knock-on effect on the reactions of the **Calvin cycle**, which relies on these products.*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

Kleptoplasty is the capacity of a non-photosynthetic host to retain functional chloroplasts from algal sources. These chloroplasts are termed kleptoplasts.

![sea-slug](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/13-photosynthesis/13-2-investigation-of-limiting-factors/assets/009-sea-slug.png)

[1]

(ii) Identify **three** key factors which may limit the rate of photosynthesis in kleptoplasts*.*

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

- Glucose can (still) be produced in times of food scarcity through photosynthesis; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Factors that may limit the rate of photosynthesis in kleptoplasts are...

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The only animals capable kleptoplasty are some marine flatworms and sea slugs belonging to the Sacoglossan clade. The root word klepto- comes from the Greek word for "thief". Organisms capable of kleptoplasty eat algae and “steal” the undigested chloroplasts. This is a bizarre phenomenon and research is still underway into how these animals can determine, within their digestive pathways, which parts are chloroplast and which is tissue for digestion. *

**Extract:**

**Fig. 2**

parts.solutionMd:
The results shown in Fig. 2 can be explained by...

- DCPIP reduced at greatest rate in red light / greatest amount of electrons excited in red light **therefore** highest rate of photosynthesis (is in red light); **[1 mark]**
- DCPIP remained in oxidised form in green light / little/few/no electrons excited in green light **therefore **lowest rate of photosynthesis (is in green light); **[1 mark]**
- DCPIP was reduced in blue light / electrons were excited in blue light **therefore **photosynthesis is occuring at a faster rate than in green light / at a slower rate than in red light; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Green light was mostly reflected by the kleptoplasts (chloroplasts) and this was seen by the highest absorbance by the colorimeter. This tells us that DCPIP remained blue and so was not reduced, meaning that little/no electrons from photosystems were excited by green light. In contrast, in red light we can see less absorbance by the colorimter, therefore this means that DCPIP lost its blue colour and was colourless, telling us that in red light photosystems reacted and released electrons which were accepted by DCPIP and it was reduced to its colourless form. When electrons are excited, photosynthesis occurs therefore the greatest rates of photosynthesis would be seen in red light. *

parts.problemMd:

Explain how solute concentration and pressure within the glomerulus establishes a water potential gradient during ultrafiltration.
parts.solutionMd:
Solute concentration and pressure within the glomerulus establishes a water potential gradient during ultrafiltration because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****six**** of the following:**

- Small solutes diffuse into the Bowman's capsule (from the blood plasma/glomerular capillaries) **and **plasma proteins are too large (to diffuse into the Bowman's capsule) / plasma proteins remain in the blood plasma as they are too large; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore the solute concentration in the blood plasma is higher than in the filtrate (in the Bowman's capsule) **OR** therefore the water potential of the blood plasma is lower than that of the filtrate (in the Bowman’s capsule); **[1 mark]**
- **So** water moves down the water potential gradient from the Bowman’s capsule into the blood plasma (in the glomerular capillaries); **[1 mark]**
- (However) blood pressure is high in the glomerulus as the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore** **the water potential of the blood plasma (in the glomerular capillaries) is higher than the water potential of the filtrate in the Bowman’s capsule; **[1 mark]**
- **So** water moves down the water potential gradient from the blood plasma (in the glomerular capillaries) into the Bowman’s capsule; **[1 mark]**
- (Overall) there is a net movement of water from the blood plasma (in the glomerular capillaries) into the Bowman’s capsule; **[1 mark]**

***Accept**** correctly named solutes for marking point 1, such as glucose*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *This can be confusing so take some time to learn the sequence of events here for both solute concentration and pressure. Although water moves in opposite directions here, there is a net movement of water into the Bowman's capsule from the blood plasma of the glomerular capillaries. *

parts.problemMd:
Research has shown that increased light intensity decreases the activity of the chemical abscisic acid (ABA) in plants.

Explain how each of the following circumstances would cause a decrease in ABA activity at increased light intensity:

(i) Electrons from chlorophyll cause an ABA precursor molecule to be converted into a chemical called zeaxanthin.

[1]

(ii) Glucose deactivates ABA.

[1]

(iii) Enzymes that break down ABA are activated at high concentrations of oxygen.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) ABA levels decrease at increased light intensity due to electrons from chlorophyll causing an ABA precursor molecule to be converted into a chemical called zeaxanthin because...

- Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll / causes photoactivation **SO** there is no precursor left to produce ABA / all of the precursor is converted into zeaxanthin (and not ABA); **[1 mark]**

(ii) ABA levels decrease at increased light intensity due to glucose deactivating ABA because...

- Light energy increases the rate of photosynthesis **SO** more glucose is produced (which deactivates ABA); **[1 mark]**

(iii) ABA levels decrease at increased light intensity due to the activation of enzymes that break down ABA at high oxygen concentrations because...

- Light energy increases the rate of photolysis **SO** more oxygen is produced/released (activating the enzymes that break down ABA); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This question relies on your knowledge of the process of photosynthesis and on you being able to apply this knowledge to an unknown context.*

> *Electrons are released from chlorophyll as a result of photoactivation, so an increase in light levels will increase the number of electrons released from chlorophyll, converting the ABA precursor into another molecule instead of into ABA; this will reduce ABA levels and therefore lead to reduced activity.*

> *Photosynthesis occurs at a higher rate when light intensity is higher; this will produce more glucose, deactivating ABA. and reducing its activity levels.*

> *Photolysis occurs at a higher rate when light intensity is higher; this will produce more oxygen, activating the enzymes that break down ABA. The enzymes will carry out their function, reducing ABA levels and therefore ABA activity.*

[1]

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The type of membrane potential in the axon at 0.5 ms is...

- Resting (potential); **[1 mark]**

> *Resting potential is negative, usually around -70mV in humans, meaning that the inside of the axon is more negative than the outside.*

(ii) Resting potential is achieved by...

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- Sodium-potassium pumps pump / use ATP to move (sodium and potassium) ions across the membrane; **[1 mark]**
- 3 sodium ions are pumped out of the axon for every 2 potassium ions that are pumped in; **[1 mark]**
- The membrane is permeable to potassium ions **SO** potassium ions diffuse out of the cell/axon; **[1 mark]**
- The membrane is less permeable to sodium **SO** sodium ions do not diffuse back in; **[1 mark]**
- Negatively charged proteins / anions are present inside the axon; **[1 mark]**

> *Resting potential is achieved primarily by the movement of ions. Sodium-potassium pumps use ATP to move more positively charged ions out of the axon than in; this causes the inside of the cell to become more negative than the outside. The movement of ions creates a concentration gradient for both sodium and potassium ions, but because the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions these diffuse back out of the cell while most sodium ions remain on the outside; this further increases the negative charge inside the cell.*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- Current flows / local circuits occur / sodium ions diffuse from the area of action potential to the next section of axon / to a section of axon at resting potential; **[1 mark]**
- Sodium ion channels (in the new section of axon) open / the membrane (in the new section of axon) depolarises; **[1 mark]**
- Hyperolarisation / the refractory period (in the previous section of axon) prevents the impulse from travelling backwards / ensures that the impulse travels in only one direction; **[1 mark]**
- In a myelinated neurone the axon is insulated / depolarisation cannot occur through the myelin / Schwann cells; **[1 mark]**
- (In a myelinated neurone) depolarisation can only occur at the nodes of Ranvier / at unmyelinated sections; **[1 mark]**
- (In a myelinated neurone) saltatory conduction occurs / the imulse jumps from one node to the next; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Marks can be gained here for describing transmission of nerve impulses in either a non-myelinated or a myelinated neurone.*

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Myelination affects the speed of nerve transmission because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****of the following:**

- Transport of ions cannot take place through the myelin sheath / Schwann cells **OR** myelin insulates the axon; **[1 mark]**
- Action potentials can only be generated at gaps between the myelin sheath / Schwann cells / at the nodes of Ranvier; **[1 mark]**
- Between the nodes/gaps sodium ions diffuse along the axon / currents flow / local circuits occur; **[1 mark]**
- (This leads to) saltatory conduction / the impulse appearing to jump between nodes (which is much faster than the transmission in an unmyelinated neurone); **[1 mark]**

> *Saltatory conduction involves the impulse appearing to jump from one node to the next; this occurs due to the diffusion of sodium ions inside the axon within the myelin sheath (know as local circuits). In an unmyelinated neurone the impulse is transmitted by the continuous process of diffusion, depolarisation, channel opeing, and sodium influx; this is much slower than the local circuits that occur within the myelin sheath.*

(ii) Axon diameter affects the speed of nerve transmission because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** of the following:**

- Wider axons have a larger (membrane) surface area across which ion transfer can take place; **[1 mark]**
- Ions diffuse into wider axons at a faster rate, creating a steeper concentration gradient within the axon (leading to faster diffusion); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.17 | 0.19 |
| 2 | 0.10 | 0.14 |
| 3 | 0.16 | 0.18 |
| 4 | 0.08 |   |
| 5 | 0.16 | 0.18 |

(i) Use the formula in Fig. 2 to complete Table 1.

[1]

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The missing cell in Table 1 is...

- 0.13 (seconds); **[1 mark]**

![may-june-2019-paper-5-q1ai---ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/013-may-june-2019-paper-5-q1ai-ma.png)

(ii) A prediction of what would happen to the reaction time if the ruler was held higher than the original set height is...

**Final answer:** **Any**** one ****of the following:**

- The reaction time would be unchanged; **[1 mark]**
- The reaction time would be longer/slower; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The first answer (reaction time unchanged) is acceptable because a person reacts to the visual stimulus of the ruler beginning to move. Therefore the height from which the ruler is dropped won't affect a person receiving a visual stimulus. An unknown is that the question does not specify how much higher the ruler would start from.*

> *The second answer (longer reaction time) is also plausible in that if the ruler is falling from a greater height, it will be travelling faster by the time student A catches it, so he/she will have to 'time' their catch to a point when the ruler has fallen to a point that is within their grasp (assuming student A keeps their hand firmly on the bench, as they should).  *

> *In our opinion this question can also be answered correctly in a third way, i.e. that the reaction times appear to get shorter. If a person catches the ruler at D=10 cm when it starts falling from D=0, then you can reasonably expect that person to catch it at D=8 cm if it starts 2 cm higher up at D=-2 cm. D=8 would give a lower reaction time when worked through the formula.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1 shows the ultrastructure of a smooth muscle cell.

![cie-ial-15-1-h-4a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/005-cie-ial-15-1-h-4a.png)

**Fig. 1**

Compare the ultrastructure of smooth muscle with that of striated muscle.
parts.solutionMd:
The ultrastructure of smooth muscle and striated muscle can be compared as follows:

*Similarities:*

- Both have a sarcolemma; **[1 mark]**
- Both have sarcoplasmic reticulum; **[1 mark]**
- Both contain overlapping actin **AND** myosin filaments; **[1 mark]**

*Differences:*

**Final answer:** **A ****maximum of three**** of the following:**

- Smooth muscle cells have a tapered/spindle shape **WHILE** striated muscle fibres are elongated; **[1 mark]**
- Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus **WHILE** striated muscle fibres are multinucleate / have multiple nuclei; **[1 mark]**
- Smooth muscle cells contain dense bodies / intermediate filaments **WHILE** striated muscle cells do not; **[1 mark]**
- Smooth muscle cells contain regions of overlapping filaments that are distributed randomly throughout the cell / that are not within myofibrils **WHILE** striated muscle contains filaments arranged in adjacent sarcomeres / in myofibrils; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The command word '**compare**' requires a summary of the similarities and/or differences between two items; here there are clearly some shared features and some distinct features when smooth muscle is compared with what you already know of striated muscle, so you should ain to **give a balance of both similarities and differences**.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1 shows the ultrastructure of a smooth muscle cell.

Smooth muscle cells contain dense bodies / intermediate filaments. Smooth muscle cells contain regions of overlapping filaments that are distributed randomly throughout the cell / that are not within myofibrils. Both smooth and striated muscle contain overlapping actin AND myosin filaments.

Use information in Fig. 1 to suggest how the actin and myosin filaments cause contraction in smooth muscle.
parts.solutionMd:
The actin and myosin filaments cause contraction in smooth muscle as follows:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- Actin and myosin filaments slide over each other / increase their overlap; **[1 mark]**
- The dense bodies are pulled / move closer together; **[1 mark]**
- The intermediate filaments pull dense bodies without attached actin and myosin closer together; **[1 mark]**
- The intermediate filaments pull on the dense bodies attached to the sarcomere to shorten the cell / squeeze the cell inwards; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You are not expected to **know** about contraction in smooth muscle, but your knowledge of muscle contraction in striated muscle, together with reasoning skills applied to Fig. 1, will allow you to answer this question.*

> *The dense bodies in a smooth muscle cell act a bit like Z lines in a sarcomere, moving towards each other when the filaments overlap. While not all dense bodies are connected by actin and myosin filaments, they are all connected to intermediate filaments, which allows the contraction of the filaments in one area of the cell to transfer to other regions of the cell in an efficient way. These filaments also connect to the sarcolemma, pulling it inwards to shorten the cell, as illustrated below:*

![contracted-smooth-muscle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/006-contracted-smooth-muscle.png)

parts.problemMd:
Smooth muscle is involved in the activities of various body systems, including the digestive system. The contraction of smooth muscle in the lining of the stomach is known to be controlled by various factors, and the nervous activity of the stomach involves a series of waves of charge known as 'gastric slow wave potentials' combined with periods of action potential. An example of this nervous activity is shown in Fig. 2 below.

![cie-ial-15-1-h-4c](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/007-cie-ial-15-1-h-4c.png)

**Fig. 2**

(i) Suggest how the slow wave potential changes at **A** and **B** in Fig. 2 are caused.

[2]

(ii) Suggest an explanation for the shape of the action potentials in Fig. 2.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The slow wave potential changes at **A** and **B** in Fig. 2 could be caused as follows:

- A = inward movement of sodium ions/Na<sup>+</sup> / calcium ions/Ca<sup>2+</sup> / potassium ions/K<sup>+</sup> **OR** outward movement of Cl<sup>-</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- B = outward movement of K<sup>+</sup> / Na+ / Ca<sup>2+</sup> **OR** inward movement of Cl<sup>-</sup>; **[1 mark]**

> *A shows a point during which the inside of the cell is becoming **more positively charged**; this could come about due to an** influx of positively charged ions** or an **efflux of negatively charged ions**.*

> *B shows the inside of the cell becoming **more negative again**; this could be the result of **outward movement of positively charged ions** or the** inward movement of negatively charged ions**.*

> *This is a suggest question, and does not expect you to know the specifics of action potentials in smooth muscle, so there are various examples of positively charged or negatively charged ions that you could list to gain the marks. The depolarisation of smooth muscle cells in the stomach is, in fact, brought about by the inward movement of calcium ions, and the repolarisation is caused by outward movement of potassium ions.*

(ii) The action potentials in Fig. 2 might occur as follows:

- Threshold potential is reached **AND** voltage gated ion channels open; **[1 mark]**
- Positively charged ions / Na<sup>+</sup> / Ca<sup>2+</sup> rush into the cell **SO** causing an action potential / spike potential; **[1 mark]**
- An action potential / peak is reach **AND** positively charged ions / K<sup>+</sup> rush out of the cell (reducing membrane potential); **[1 mark]**
- This process repeats several times until the membrane potential drops back below the threshold; **[1 mark]**

> *While the events in a smooth muscle are not, in fact, exactly the same as those in the neurones that you will have learned about, this question is another suggest question, leaving you free to apply the knowledge that you do have to this unusual set of action potentials. For full marks here you must acknowledge the repeating nature of the action potentials shown in Fig. 2.*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Smooth muscle in the stomach is classified as 'single-unit' smooth muscle, while smooth muscle in other parts of the body, e.g. the iris of the eye, is 'multi-unit' smooth muscle. Fig. 3 below shows a difference in the neurone connections within single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle.

![cie-ial-15-1-h-4d](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/008-cie-ial-15-1-h-4d.png)

**Fig. 3**

(i) Suggest how the initiation of muscle contraction differs between single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle.

[2]

(ii) Suggest how the roles of single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle may differ.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The initiation of muscle contraction differs between single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle as follows:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- In single-unit smooth muscle each cell is stimulated to contract by the release of neurotransmitters / the binding of neurotransmitters to receptors **WHILE** in multi-unit smooth muscle some cells are stimulated by neurotransmitters / neurotransmitter binding and other cells are stimulated by neighbouring cells / by the movement of ions through gap junctions; **[1 mark]**
- In single-unit smooth muscle each cell is stimulated individually **WHILE** in multi-unit smooth muscle cells are stimulated as a group; **[1 mark]**
- In single-unit smooth muscle all of the cells can initiate contraction at the same time **WHILE** in multi-unit smooth muscle the cells nearest to the neurones will contract first (and cells that are further away will take longer to contract); **[1 mark]**

> *In single-unit smooth muscle the neurones and varicosities are distributed throughout the tissue, meaning that neurotransmitters released from the vesicles can diffuse directly to receptors on the surface of each individual cell. By contrast, in multi-unit smooth muscle only the outer layer of cells can receive neurotransmitter signals, but the cells themselves are connected by structures labelled 'gap junctions'; this means that the contraction passes from cell-to-cell, rather than an impulse being sent directly from the neurone.*

(ii) The roles of single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle may differ as follows:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** of the following:**

- Single-unit smooth muscle is involved with small motions / movements that require fine control **WHILE** multi-unit smooth muscle is involved with large motions / movements that do not require fine control / movements that only need gross control; **[1 mark]**
- Single-unit smooth muscle is involved with localised movement / movement in a single location **WHILE** multi-unit smooth muscle is involved with waves of movement (e.g. stomach churning / peristalsis); **[1 mark]**

***Accept**** 'single-unit smooth muscle is involved with small*<u>*er*</u>* motions' ****OR ****'multi-unit muscle is involved with larg*<u>*er*</u>* motions' for marking point 1.*

> *The different mechanisms for initiating contraction of smooth muscle indicate that these different types of muscle have different roles; muscle cells that can receive individual instructions to contract allow a high level of control over which sections of muscle contract at any given time, while muscle cells receiving and passing on impulses from other muscle cells results in a wave of contraction, such as when food is pushed along the digestive tract by peristalsis, or when the heart contracts from the base upwards (though note that cardiac muscle is not exactly the same as smooth muscle).*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Botulinum toxin is sometimes used in the treatment of migraine headaches. In a study investigating the effect of botulinum toxin treatment on severe migraines, 30 individuals were randomly assigned to either a botulinum toxin treatment or a control treatment. The participants reported their frequency of severe migraines at day 0, before receiving a single round of treatment, administered by intramuscular injection. Participants were then assessed again at 30 days, 60 days and 90 days.

Fig. 2 below shows the results of the study.

![Graph showing the effect of botulinum vs control treatments on migraine frequency over 90 days](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-1-control-and-coordination-in-mammals/assets/010-graph-showing-the-effect-of-botulinum-vs-control.png)

**Fig. 2**

A medical student read the study findings and concluded that a single round of botulinum toxin injections was a suitable treatment for severe migraine.

Assess the student's conclusion.
parts.solutionMd:
An assessment of the conclusion that 'a single round of botulinum toxin injections is a suitable treatment for severe migraine' could include:

*In support of the conclusion:*

- Patients that receive botulinum toxin have significantly fewer migraines than patients receiving the control treatment from day 30 to day 90; **[1 mark]**
- There is only a 1 % probability that the difference between treatment and control at day 60 is due to chance **OR** there is only a 2 % probability that the difference between treatment and control at day 90 is due to chance; **[1 mark]**
- The use of a control group shows that the difference is due to the botulinum treatment and not any other factor; **[1 mark]**

*Against the conclusion:*

**Final answer:** **A maximum of ****three**** of the following:**

- The probability that the difference is due to chance is 5 % / relatively high at day 30 OR p = 0.05 is not considered statistically significant in a medical trial **SO** the treatment takes a long time / more than 30 days to be effective; **[1 mark]**
- The probability that the difference in results is due to chance increases between day 60 and day 90 **OR** the difference between botulinum and control treatments is no longer (medically) significant after 90 days; **[1 mark]**
- The effects of the treatment may wear off after 90 days / there is no evidence to show the efficacy of the treatment after 90 days; **[1 mark]**
- A sample of 30 individuals may not be representative of all migraine sufferers; **[1 mark]**
- Different participants may have a different definition of severe migraine / the definition of severe migraine is subjective; **[1 mark]**
- This is only a single study **SO** would need to be replicated / more data would be needed to support the conclusion; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The command word 'assess' requires you to make an informed judgement. When assessing a conclusion that has been drawn from data, a structured approach is to consider factors that show support, or that may argue against, the conclusion.*

> *This question requires a good understanding of statistical analysis. Normally as biologists we look for differences in data that are significant at the **5 % probability level (p = 0.05)**, meaning that there is **only a 5 % probability that any difference is due to chance**; this is acceptable when dealing with data that relate to, e.g. genetic crosses, or studies of ecology.*

> *Data that are significantly different at a lower probability level, e.g. 1 % (p = 0.01) or 2 % (p = 0.02) as shown here, are even less likely to show a difference that is due to chance alone. In medical trials a p value of 0.01 is used, meaning that there **cannot be more than a 1 % probability that any difference is due to chance**. While you are **not** necessarily expected to be aware of this, you should still notice that the difference between treatment and control groups becomes more significant between day 30 and day 60, but then decreases in significance between day 60 and day 90.*

> *Don't forget to consider aspects of experimental design when considering the validity of a conclusion, e.g. here the sample size is small, and the study has not been replicated by other researchers.*

parts.problemMd:
Botulinum toxin is a neurotoxin produced by *Clostridium botulinum* bacteria. Neurotoxins are produced by several other groups of organisms, for example in the venom of snakes and some invertebrates. Table 1 gives some examples of different types of neurotoxins and describes the action of each toxin within cells. **Table 1** | **Toxin** | **Found in** | **Effect on cells** | |---|---|---| | Dendrotoxin | Snake venom, e.g. black mamba | - Blocks potassium channels at nodes of Ranvier
- Blocks voltage-gated potassium channels | | α-Bungarotoxin | Snake venom, e.g. many-banded krait snake | - Binds irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors | | Agatoxin | Spider venom, e.g. funnel web spider | - Blocks voltage gated sodium channels
- Blocks calcium channels | Explain how each of the following toxins would impact nerve impulses: (i) Dendrotoxin [2] (ii) α-Bungarotoxin [2] (iii) Agatoxin [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Dendrotoxin will affect nerve impulses as follows:

- Slow down speed of transmission; **[1 mark]**
- The membrane will not depolarise at the nodes of Ranvier **SO **saltatory conduction will not occur; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Neurones will be constantly stimulated/depolarised / stuck in action potential; **[1 mark]**
- Potassium ions will be unable to leave the axon **SO** repolarisation will not take place; **[1 mark]**

(ii) α-Bungarotoxin will affect nerve impulses as follows:

- Nerve impulses will not be transmitted across synapses / no action potentials will be generated in postsynaptic cells; **[1 mark]**
- Acetylcholine will be unable to bind to receptors **SO** there will be no influx of sodium in the postsynaptic cell; **[1 mark]**

(iii) Agatoxins will affect nerve impulses as follows:

- There will be no generation of action potentials; **[1 mark]**
- Sodium ion influx (at the point at which threshold potential is reached) is prevented **SO** the membrane will not depolarise beyond threshold potential; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- No neurotransmitter will be released into the synaptic cleft; **[1 mark]**
- Calcium ions will not move into presynaptic cell **SO** no vesicles (of neurotransmitter) will move towards / bind to the presynaptic membrane; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Electrical activity occurs in living organisms as the result of the movement of charged particles, or ions, across cell membranes. The reversal of electrical charge across a cell membrane is known as depolarisation.

Plant cells can also be depolarised. The cells of the sensitive Mimosa plant, *Mimosa pudica*, can become depolarised in response to a touch stimulus. Fig. 2.1 shows the first two stages of depolarisation in *M. pudica.*

![15-2-fig-2-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/15-control-and-coordination/15-2-control-and-coordination-in-plants/assets/001-15-2-fig-2-1.png)

**Fig. 1**

(i) Suggest how the cells of *M. pudica* become depolarised in the next stage of the process shown in Fig. 1.

[2]

(ii) Suggest how the cells of *M. pudica* might become repolarised to return to a resting state.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The cells of *M. pudica* become depolarised in the next stage of the process shown in Fig. 1 by...

- Chloride ions diffuse out of the cell / move out of the cell down a concentration gradient; **[1 mark]**
- The loss of negatively charged ions causes the inside of the cell to become more positive; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Repolarisation could occur by...

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** of the following:**

- The opening of potassium ion channels (in response to depolarisation); **[1 mark]**
- Potassium ions diffusing out of the cell; **[1 mark]**
- The loss of positively charged ions causes the inside of the cell to become more negative / restores the resting state; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This is quite a tricky question, but you have been given quite a lot of information in Fig. 1 and you should be able to apply what you know about depolarisation in animal cells and in venus fly traps.*

> *Depolarisation involves the inside of the cell becoming more positive; this can be achieved either by a gain of positively charged ions or a loss of negatively charged ions. In this case, you have been told that a stimulus leads to the opening of chloride ions and Fig. 1 shows chloride ions inside the cell; it is, therefore, logical to think that an outward movement of negatively charged chloride ions causes depolarisation.*

> *You already know that an outward movement of potassium ions leads to repolarisation in animal neurones. Fig. 1 shows potassium ions and a corresponding potassium ion channel. Logic says that the opening of the channel would lead to the outward movement of positive potassium ions, restoring resting potential.*

parts.problemMd: Describe the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis.
parts.solutionMd:
The behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis involves...

**Final answer:** **Any ****eight**** of the following:**

*Meiosis I*

- Chromosomes condense; **[1 mark]**
- Homologous chromosomes pair up / bivalents form; **[1 mark]**
- Crossing over occurs / chiasmata form; **[1 mark]**
- Spindle fibres/microtubules attach to centromeres; **[1 mark]**
- Bivalents/pairs line up on equator of cell; **[1 mark]**
- Independent assortment (of homologous pairs); **[1 mark]**
- Chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles; **[1 mark]**
- Chromosome number is halved / cell becomes haploid; **[1 mark]**

*Meiosis II*

- (Individual) chromosomes line up on equator; **[1 mark]**
- Chromosomes line up at right-angles to the equator from meiosis I; **[1 mark]**
- Centromeres break/divide; **[1 mark]**
- (Sister) chromatids separate; **[1 mark]**

***Accept ****general statements such as "meiosis halves the chromosome number / produces haploid cells" without the specific context of meiosis I for marking point 8. *

***Reject**** statements that suggest that the halving of the chromosome number occurs specifically during meiosis II.*

**[Total: 8 marks]**

> *This question refers specifically to the **behaviour of chromosomes**, so descriptions of other cell components such as nuclear membranes and centrioles will not be credited.*

> *Make sure that you are confident at distinguishing between **bivalents**, **single chromosomes**, and **chromatids**:*

- *Bivalent = a homologous **pair** of chromosomes*
- *Chromosome = a **single** chromosome. Until anaphase of meiosis II this will consist of **two sister chromatids** joined at the centromere and will have an 'X-shaped' appearance.*
- *Chromatid = one of the two identical halves of a chromosome formed during DNA replication in preparation for cell division. Joined chromatids are referred to as 'sister chromatids' or 'a chromosome'. As soon as the sister chromatids are separated during meiosis II they become chromosomes in their own right.*

> *Note that cells** become haploid** at the end of **meiosis I** when the **bivalents** are separated. At the end of meiosis II the **amount of DNA **in the cell halves when the chromatids are separated but the ploidy of the cell does not change. It is still correct to say that 'meiosis produces haploid cells', but not to say that 'meiosis II halves the chromosome number'.*

parts.solutionMd:
Edwards syndrome affects every cell in the body because...

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Mutations occur in individual cells during DNA replication all the time, but these single cells have little impact on an individual; genetic disorders result when the mutation occurs at the gamete stage. Gametes fuse to form the zygote, which then divides by mitosis to form the rest of the cells in a living organism. Any mutation present in the zygote will therefore be copied every time mitosis occurs, meaning that every cell in the body will contain the original mutation.*

Describe how these results are different from the expected results **and** explain why they are different.
parts.solutionMd:
These results are different from the expected results because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****five ****of the following:**

- The expected ratio was 1:1:1:1 / the ratio is not 1:1:1:1; **[1 mark]**
- The flies are mostly grey(body)-red(eye) and black(body)-brown(eye); **[1 mark]**
- The majority resemble (original) parents / have parental phenotypes; **[1 mark]**
- There is a 1:1 ratio of two parental types **AND** a 1:1 ratio of recombinant types; **[1 mark]**
- Genes (for eye colour and body colour) are linked / on same chromosome; **[1 mark]**
- (alleles) G+R linked and g+r linked (in F1 / heterozygotes); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *It is worth bearing in mind that when offspring ratios do not match the expected ratios it is often due to the effects of **linkage**.*

> *When genes are linked they are found at **different loci on the same chromosome**. This means that when chromosomes are separated during meiosis I the alleles at these loci are much more likely to be **inherited together**. This leads to offspring that have the same traits as their parents.*

> *Any offspring that have a combination of traits that should not theoretically be possible (given the linkage of the genes) must have come about as a result of **crossing over**; alleles are exchanged, producing new allele combinations. In certain species of bacteria, such as *Escherichia coli*, transcription of the structural genes of the lac operon enables the production of lactase. This process only occurs in the presence of lactose, and is also affected by the presence or absence of glucose.

In the absence of glucose, *E.coli* cells produce the molecule cAMP. cAMP binds to a catabolite activator protein (CAP), activating it and allowing it to bind to a region of the lac operon known as the CAP site. The presence of the CAP protein makes it easier for RNA polymerase to bind and greatly increases the transcription rate of the structural genes. RNA polymerase does not bind well to the promoter in the absence of CAP.

Fig. 1 illustrates the effect of CAP on the transcription rate of the structural genes.

![16-3-fig-2-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-biology-25/16-inheritance/16-3-gene-control/assets/004-16-3-fig-2-1.png)

**Fig. 1**

(i) Explain why the structural genes are transcribed in the presence of lactose.

[3]

(ii) Suggest how the transcription of the structural genes would be affected if *E.coli* was grown in a medium that contained both glucose **and** lactose.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The structural genes are transcribed in the presence of lactose because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- Lactose is taken up by the *E. coli /* bacterial cells; **[1 mark]**
- Lactose binds to the repressor protein; **[1 mark]**
- This distorts / changes the shape of the repressor protein; **[1 mark]**
- The repressor protein cannot bind to the operator (meaning that RNA polymerase can bind to the promoter); **[1 mark]**

*Ignore references to RNA polymerase and transcription as this information has already been given in the question.*

(ii) If *E. coli* was grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose...

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- cAMP would not be produced (due to the presence of glucose) **AND** would not bind to CAP; **[1 mark]**
- CAP would not be activated **AND** would not bind to the CAP site; **[1 mark]**
- The transcription rate (of structural genes) would be low (since RNA polymerase would not bind very well to the promoter); **[1 mark]**
- A small amount of lactase would be produced; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *This is a tricky question that requires you to use your knowledge of the effect of lactose on the lac operon at the same as applying new information about the effects of glucose. *

> *You know that in the presence of lactose the repressor protein cannot bind to the operator and RNA polymerase can therefore bind to the promoter and initiate transcription of the structural genes.*

> *However, at the same time as these familiar events, you have also been told that the presence or absence of glucose can affect this process. The presence of glucose means that cAMP is not produced and that CAP is not activated. The absence of CAP at the CAP site means that even though RNA polymerase is theoretically free to bind (due to the absence of the repressor protein) it actually cannot bind very well. This means that there will be some transcription of the structural genes but not very much, and only a small amount of lactose would be produced.*

> *This is beneficial to the bacteria because it prevents them from producing too much lactase when glucose is available as a preferred energy source.*

Fig. 1 shows the structure of the trp operon in the presence of high tryptophan levels.

Using the information in Fig. 1, explain the effect of high tryptophan levels on the trp operon.
parts.solutionMd:
High tryptophan levels will have the following effect on the trp operon...

**Final answer:** **Any ****four**** of the following:**

- Tryptophan/Trp binds to the trp repressor protein; **[1 mark]**
- This causes a change in the (trp repressor) protein shape/conformation **SO** allowing it to bind to the operator; **[1 mark]**
- RNA polymerase cannot bind to the operator/DNA (due to the presence of the repressor protein); **[1 mark]**
- This (binding) prevents the transcription of the structural genes **OR** the enzymes needed for the production of tryptophan cannot be synthesised; **[1 mark]**
- Tryptophan will not be produced (due to the absence of the enzymes needed for its synthesis); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The trp operon functions in a similar way to the **lac** operon, except that in this case the presence of high levels of tryptophan will repress the expression of the structural genes in order to regulate the amount of tryptophan in the bacterial cell. It would be a waste of energy to synthesise tryptophan when levels are already high.*

(i) The enzymes produced by the structural genes of the trp operon can be classified as:

- Repressible (enzymes); **[1 mark]**

(ii) The reason for this is that...

- The binding of the trp repressor protein to the operator/ will prevent/repress the synthesis of the enzymes / prevent/repress the transcription of the genes coding for the enzymes; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

The trp operon can be regulated by another mechanism called attenuation; this involves a leader transcript, *trpL*. When tryptophan levels are high attenuation causes RNA polymerase to end the transcription of the structural genes prematurely.

- The tertiary/3D structure of the resulting proteins would be altered **OR **the shape of the enzyme active site would be altered / the active site would no longer be complementary to the substrate (and tryptophan would no longer be produced); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The hormone oestrogen can diffuse into human body cells. parts.solutionMd:
Transcription means....

- A complementary copy of the DNA template strand is produced **OR** one strand of the DNA molecule acts as a template; **[1 mark]**
- The mRNA/messenger RNA contains the information for the synthesis of a polypeptide/protein / can be translated into a polypeptide/protein; **[1 mark]**

In certain types of breast cancer ER is no longer regulated by control mechanisms and may lead to the development of oestrogen induced tumours. Tamoxifen was one of the first effective treatments for these types of cancers and is still used with great success.

- Tamoxifen is not complementary in shape to the cofactor (protein); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain how transcription factors stimulate the expression of a gene.
parts.solutionMd:

- This initiates transcription of the gene **OR** transcription can then begin **OR** mRNA can then join by complementary base pairing to the gene sequence; **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
We can compare the action of oestrogen and non-competitive inhibitors as follows...

- Oestrogen binds to a receptor on the transcription factor** in the same way** **as **a non-competitive inhibitor binds to an alternative/allosteric site on an enzyme; **[1 mark]**
- Binding to the receptor triggers a change to the shape of the transcription factor **in the same way** **as** binding to the alternative/allosteric site on an enzyme causes a change in the active site shape;** [1 mark]**
- (However), non-competitive inhibitor inhibits enzyme function, **whereas **oestrogen stimulates gene expression **OR** a non-competitive inhibitor prevents the enzyme from forming enzyme-substrate complexes, **whereas **oestrogen stimulates the attachment of the transcriptional factor to the DNA; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Oestrogen can enter the cell cytoplasm across the phospholipid bilayer because it is lipid soluble. Once in the cytoplasm, it can bind to the transcription factor which allows the transcription factor to bind to a specific site on the DNA. This will initiate transcription. Linking this mechanism back to the topic of enzymes, non-competitive inhibitors work by binding to the enzyme to cause a change to the tertiary structure and therefore the shape of the active site so that the enzyme can no longer form enzyme-substrate complexes.*

> *Be sure to use comparative language in your answer so you show the examiner you understand the two processes being compared and contrasted. *

- Different alleles at a single locus have a small effect on the phenotype in continuous variation **WHILE** it will have a large effect on the phenotype in discontinuous variation; **[1 mark]**

- A large number of genes / polygenes may have a combined effect on the phenotype in continuous variation **WHILE** a smaller number of genes may have an effect on the phenotype in discontinuous variation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember when a question asks you to contrast two concepts, you must focus on the main differences between them. In this case, you must make mention of both continuous and discontinuous variation in your answer to receive the marks.*

From the data described in part (c), calculate the t value between the data from Country A and Country B.

The formula for calculating *t* is as follows:

$t = \frac{\left| \bar{x}_{1} - \bar{x}_{2} \right|}{\sqrt{( \frac{s_{1}^{2} }{n_{1} } + \frac{s_{2}^{2} }{n_{2} } )}}$
parts.solutionMd:
The calculation of t is as follows:

- Numerator:  difference in means = 21.03 - 19.94 = 1.09; **[1 mark]**
- Denominator: squares of SDs divided by sample sizes = $\sqrt{\frac{1.687^{2}}{10}+\frac{0.756^{2}}{10}}=0.585$ ; **[1 mark]**
- Value of* t* = 1.09 ÷ 0.585 = 1.86; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: State the purpose of the Hardy Weinberg equation.
parts.solutionMd:

- Calculate/work out allele frequency/frequencies **OR** genotype frequency/frequencies (in a population); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The Hardy Weinberg principle states that the genetics of a population will remain constant from one generation to the next provided that certain conditions, or assumptions, are met.

State **three** of the assumptions made by the Hardy Weinberg principle.
parts.solutionMd:
Assumptions made by the Hardy Weinberg principle include...

**Final answer:** **Any ****three**** of the following:**

- Mating is random; **[1 mark]**
- No natural selection is taking place; **[1 mark]**
- No gene flow with other populations / migration / immigration / new individuals entering the population / emigration / individuals leaving the population; **[1 mark]**
- No mutation is occurring; **[1 mark]**
- The population is large / no genetic drift is taking place; **[1 mark]**
- Organisms are diploid; **[1 mark]**
- Only sexual reproduction is taking place / no asexual reproduction is taking place; **[1 mark]**
- Generations do not overlap; **[1 mark]**
- Allele frequencies are the same between males and females; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *There are many marks up for grabs here so focus on the assumptions that you will find the easiest to remember.*

parts.problemMd:
One of the Hardy Weinberg equations is given below.

*p + q = 1*

State what is represented by ***p*** in this equation.
parts.solutionMd:
In this equation ***p*** represents...

- The <u>frequency</u> of the <u>dominant</u> allele; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *The frequency of all of the alleles in a population is 1, or 100 %, so the frequencies of the dominant and recessive alleles must add up to this total, hence **p + q = 1**.*

parts.problemMd:
A group of biologists conducted an investigation on a remote archipelago (a collection of islands) in the Atlantic Ocean. They measured the claw length of a large number of mice of a single species living on the islands. The mouse species had no natural predators.

After the biologists' visit to the islands, a species of snake that preyed on the mice was accidentally introduced on half of the islands. These snakes were not able to climb trees but they could move very fast over open ground. Several years after the snakes were introduced the biologists returned and found that the claw length of the mice on the snake infested islands had increased while the claw length of the mice on the islands without snakes remained unchanged. The longer claws enabled the mice to climb trees, while shorter claws enabled them to run faster.

State the purpose of including the islands where no snakes were present in the biologists' investigation.
parts.solutionMd:
The purpose of the islands without snakes was...

- (To serve) as a control; **[1 mark]**
- To demonstrate that the claw length (of the mice) remained unchanged in the absence of snakes **OR** to demonstrate that the presence of snakes (and not any other variable) led to an increase in claw length; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *In scientific investigations, the control is the test group that does not receive treatment. Without the control group there would be nothing to compare the treatment group to, and therefore no way of being sure that the change observed in the dependent variable (in this case the claw length of the mice) is due to the experimental treatment (the presence of snakes).*

parts.problemMd:
A mutation in the gene controlling claw length in mice was responsible for the development of longer claws in the mice in part a).

Explain how a mutation could lead to a change in claw length in mice.
parts.solutionMd:
A mutation could lead to a change in claw length by...

- (A mutation) changes the base sequence / triplet code (of DNA); **[1 mark]**
- (A mutation) may result in a new <u>allele</u>; **[1 mark]**
- The new allele codes for a different protein / a protein with an altered structure (which affects the growth/length of the claws); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *A short diffusion distance*

parts.problemMd: Distinguish between the biological terms *niche* and *ecosystem*.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) is the world's largest global environmental organisation. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species™ evaluates the conservation status of plant and animal species.

parts.solutionMd:
The consequences on genetic biodiversity of having a wild population of just six birds would be

**Final answer:** **Any ****four ****of the following:**

- Low/decreased (genetic) diversity/variation; **[1 mark]**
- Low/decreased heterozygosity; **[1 mark]**
- Harmful recessive alleles may come together; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Inbreeding depression</u>; **[1 mark]**
- No/decreased <u>hybrid vigour</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Not/less able to adapt to changed selection pressure/environment; **[1 mark]**

> *Small populations have low **genetic diversity** due to the low total number of alleles of each gene present in the population. This increases the risk of any offspring inheriting** two identical alleles** from their parents (this reduces **heterozygosity**), which can then further reduce the genetic diversity in the next generation. Inheriting two identical copies of a gene also increases the risk of inheriting **two harmful recessive alleles**, leading to the problem of **inbreeding depression**.*

> *Populations with low genetic diversity are less likely to be able to adapt (by natural selection) to a changing environment, and are therefore more likely to be wiped out by such change.*

parts.problemMd: Describe the method by which genetic fingerprinting (also known as DNA fingerprinting or DNA profiling) is undertaken.
parts.solutionMd:
Genetic fingerprinting is carried out as follows...

**Final answer:** **Any ****five**** of the following:**

- DNA is extracted/isolated from a sample (e.g. cheek cell, root of a hair, blood, semen); **[1 mark]**
- DNA is copied/increased/amplified through <u>PCR</u> / the <u>polymerase chain reaction</u>; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Outline the key steps involved in the commercial production of human recombinant insulin.
